idiom_name: service struct over consumer-defined interfaces, explicit *sql.Tx threaded through the call
implementation_notes: Go has no DI container and no annotations, so the layer is a hand-written struct (or a package of methods) whose collaborators are small interfaces declared by the consumer, and the transaction is an explicit *sql.Tx from db.BeginTx(ctx, nil) that is passed to every call which must participate - with defer tx.Rollback() as the guard and an explicit Commit as the end. Nothing replaces the classic structure; Go's conventions simply strip it to the minimum: one package per service, methods named after use cases, dependencies passed to the constructor function. The structure is still justified when several adapters (HTTP handler, CLI, queue worker) call the same operations; for a single adapter, a handler calling repositories directly is idiomatic.
pitfalls: Any call that uses the *sql.DB instead of the *sql.Tx executes outside the transaction, so every collaborator must accept the transaction explicitly.
defer tx.Rollback() after a successful Commit returns ErrTxDone - ignore the error deliberately, or it masks the real result.
Cancelling the context passed to BeginTx rolls the transaction back automatically, but only if that same context is threaded through the whole call chain.
